speechtext:
This bill was widely circulated throughout Canada and the question arose that inasmuch as it specifically provided for an appeal from a decision in the Yukon territory, that might seem to imply that there should be no appeal from any provincial court,
and it was deemed advisable to make it clear that 'there may be an appeal from a provincial court to the Supreme Court of Canada in order that the procedure under this measure may be regulated, if necessary, by the same judicial authority, throughout all the provinces. I therefore propose this amendment which will be moved by the Minister of National Revenue:
That section 14 of Bill No. 77 be struck out anti the following substituted therefor:
14. An appeal shall, by leave of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, lie to that court from the highest court of final resort in or for the province or territory in which the proceeding originated.
2.	The Supreme Court of Canada shall have jurisdiction to hear and and to decide according to its ordinary procedure any appeal so permitted and to award costs.
3.	No such appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada shall operate as a stay of proceedings unless the judge who permits such appeal shall so order, and to the extent to which he shall order, and the appellant shall not be required to provide any security for costs, hut unless he provides security for costs, in an amount to be fixed by the judge permitting the appeal, he shall not be awarded costs in the event of his success upon such appeal.
4.	The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada on any such appeal shall be final and conclusive.
This same provision appears in the Bankruptcy Act in section 178 and also in the act with respect to the winding up of companies. I am introducing no new provision. The theory of the Bankruptcy Act with regard to giving security for costs was this, that, though a bankrupt who might have good grounds for an appeal might not be able to provide the security for such an appeal, his right of appeal was maintained, but, in case he gave no security for an appeal to the other party, he could not obtain costs even if the decision on the appeal were given in his favour. That is a principle which has been enacted in other statutes, but particularly in the Bankruptcy Act, and in order to make it clear I am suggesting this amendment which my colleague the Minister of National Revenue will move.

My amendment however was ruled out of order. Upon this occasion I should like to outline one or two of the criticisms made against proposals I submitted to ithe committee. This house has given compensation to employees who have left the service of the government. Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words to say on this bill. I made some observations when the bill was in committee, but I have something else to say now in regard to the colonization scheme of the railways. The other day the Minister of Labour read a letter from Mr. J. E. Laforce, colonization agent of the Canadian National Railways. That gentleman lives in Montreal. He says the condition of the settlers throughout the country is very good. Sir, the only observation I have to make about this colonization scheme is that it is a mixup. Too many cooks spoil the broth. We have people engaged by the province, others employed by the railway company and others employed by the federal government. The first land grants that were made to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were mostly in the west, and after these grants were made by the Macdonald government the Canadian Pacific was interested in settling the western plains, and there we have the beginnings of immigration in this country. Afterward they had a steamship company that carried immigrants from other countries to Canada, and thus immigration came mostly to the west. Now that that field for immigration is closed to a certain extent they have a colonization scheme for the wild parts of the eastern provinces. I wonder what the real instructions are that are given to Mr. Laforce, and what is the work done by him. He writes letters that are like school-boys' exercises, published in many papers, telling people that they should go back to the land. Every time there is a complaint about the way settlers are treated in this country we have a letter from Mr. Laforce painting everything in rose-pink colours, saying these settlers are not suffering at all. The other day a paper in Montreal
C .N.R.-C .P.R .-Mr. Pouliot

said I should be more careful about securing affidavits from settlers in the north. I did not write first to these men. I did not know them. They wrote to me telling me about their troubles. And the Minister of Labour answers with a letter from Mr. Laforce saying everything is well in the best possible world. I have no petty political motive in this matter, but what I find strange is that when people are suffering and enduring hardship we have this gentleman writing to the Minister of Labour in Ottawa or to the Minister of Colonization in Quebec, saying that everything is going well. I am surprised. I wonder if that gentleman is working to keep his job. I do not see why a colonization scheme organized by the Canadian National Railways is putting people twenty miles from a main highway. Not only twenty miles from the main automobile highway, but farther than that from the railway. They are sent out as prisoners were during the war, worse off than prisoners in concentration camps-not those in this country because here they were fairly well treated, but in other countries, Germany for instance.
I would like to have the truth about the whole matter. As the Minister of Labour is interested in it, because he subscribes to it; as the Minister of Railways is interested because he has the high supervision of all business done by the Canadian National Railways; as the Minister of Colonization for Quebec is interested also, because some of his employees put these people on the land, I ask them to stand together in order to get the truth of the matter. I appeal to the kind heart of the Minister of Railways, as I did to the kind heart of the Minister of Labour, that they will together arrange to ascertain the truth of the matter at once, and, if these people need food, to supply it to them. I ask the^ Minister of Railways to see to it that, if their employees paint everything in pink in order to keep their jobs, justice shall be done to them, and if they give unreliable reports that they shall be dealt with at once.
Sir, I do not wish to insist on this point any longer. I bring it to the attention of the house for the last time this session, and I hope the good influence of the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Colonization in Quebec will be exerted to see that the right system is provided for these settlers in the north.
Then I have one more thing to say in regard to the trustees of the Canadian National Railways. I do not know who they may be, and if I have used vehement language in this house it was to prevent a bad appointment to the board. I leave it to the wisdom

of the government to appoint fairminded men, independent in character, and having experience that qualifies them to achieve success. Then I have a warning to give to the trustees. If we want to trade with other countries we need vessels and steamship lines. We have very good steamships in the Canadian National fleet, such as the Lady Nelson and other ships of that class. Now with a smaller trade moving there is an increase in unfair and cutthroat competition by private concerns. Every member of the government knows what I allude to. In the maritime provinces, especially in Halifax, there are private firms who try to discriminate against the Canadian National steamships. It is a well known fact, it is superfluous for me to give names, but I warn the government and the trustees against those private firms who want to destroy the trade of the Canadian National steamships between Canada and the [DOT] West Indies.
My last word is that I hope the trustees will give a fair hearing to complaints of employees who have been suffering injustice in the past, will see to it that they have no grievances in the future. For instance, an engine exploded on the Transcontinental railway . not far from Quebec. Why? Because no sufficient inspection was made at the shops. Those who are responsible for that lack of inspection are really guilty of manslaughter, whether they be high officials of the Canadian National railways or whoever they. are. May I tell them that it is most important for efficient and economical operation that the rolling stock of the railway be kept in good repair, instead of indulging in high capital expenditures. It will save money to the railway and supply work for the men.

Mr. Speaker, may I add my word of support to the amendment that has just been moved. I do so not only because I am in favour of the principle enunciated therein, but because I realize more and more that this house and this country will have to recognize in the near future that industry, private industry, must be made more responsible for the well-being of the persons who are employed in it. I recollect that it is not long ago that the Minister of Railways himself made a very eloquent plea at a public meeting, suggesting precisely that principle, that industry could not and must not be permitted to discard its men in the callous, cold-blooded way in which men have been and are being discarded by industry. In my opinion the human element in production is more sacred than dividends or profits. The welfare of the

C.N.R ,-C.P.11.-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
men and women in industry should come before the interests of the investors. Until that principle is recognized we are not going to have either justice or safety in this country.
There is one other matter to which I desire to direct the attention of the minister and the house. That is, within the ranks of the Canadian National system at this moment there are men who are almost directly responsible for any disgrace that may have come upon the system in the last few years and who still hold remunerative positions, who have not been corrected, disciplined or dismissed. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, for over two and a half years this system has been subjected to not only an unfair but a very striking and prolonged attack, and the result has been to bring into disrepute the whole principle of public ownership and the management of the national system. The men themselves feel very hurt in regard to this matter, especially in view of the fact that the principle itself has not been successfully assailed, and because most of the criticism that has been directed against the national system should have been directed against individuals connected with the administration thereof. As for the rank and file of the men, all hon. members have been very generous in their praise, and I can only attribute to them the highest zeal, the greatest efficiency and the most praiseworthy loyalty. It is not the rank and file of the men who are to blame; there are some men on the staff who have not been as zealous in regard to the public interest and the welfare of the Canadian National system as they might have been, and it is to those few individuals that I wish to address my remarks at this time.
Within the ranks of the technical staff, Mr. Speaker, there are some men who should be brought to book. There are persons in that department upon whom much blame should rest. The engineering department of any railway system is one of the most important departments. The engineering department of the Canadian National, as is the case with some other roads, has almost complete control over construction. The operating and mechanical departments of this line, so far as I can ascertain, have nothing to do with the actual construction of branch lines, and that has been the case particularly in western Canada. The construction department of the western division is under the immediate supervision of the chief engineer of western lines at Winnipeg, and under the general control of the chief engineer at headquarters. This construction department had its origin back in the old Mackenzie and Mann days, and it
has been maintained by the chief engineer of western lines almost unchanged since that time. It was carried into the so called public ownership form of operation and was continued even during the period of little or no construction. It was used exclusively in the rehabilitation and construction of the Hudson Bay railway, and looked after the construction of branch lines in the west. It was permitted to become very much over-staffed; the organization embraced within its ambit not only engineers but engineers of various and terrible designations. We had engineering experts, supervising engineers, specialty engineers and so on. What has been the result of all this overloading of the technical staff? The Duff report definitely indicates what has been the result. I wish hon. members would turn to page 21 of that report and study paragraph 54, which discloses probably the greatest single source of waste in connection with Canadian National historj' in our time. The Duff report says:
It will be observed that the average cost per mile in the case of the Canadian National has shown a progressive increase rising from $40,214 to $51,640 over the period, while the average cost per mile of the Canadian Pacific over tile same period has declined from $35,470 to $30,229. The cost of individual branch lines varies not only as between the two systems but as between branches of the same system; nevertheless, a majority of the lines were built in similar territory for like purposes. This difference in costs represents an addition to the annual interest charge of almost $800 per mile.
It must be clear, Mr. Speaker, to any student of railway affairs that an unjustifiable overload of that kind places the Canadian National system in almost a hopeless position. I wonder what has been done; I wonder why these men remain on the staff. After all the chief engineer of the western division must have been responsible for the specifications and construction at the time these lines were built which showed the appalling increase commented upon in the Duff report. I am at a loss to understand why such men should escape while the loyal, hardworking, efficient member of the running trades or the maintenance or operating staff is fired out on his ear without thought of compensation.
It may be suggested that the character of the country through which the lines were constructed differs, but that is not the case; the Duff report so states. It may be argued that construction on the Canadian National was better than construction on the Canadian Pacific, but that argument will not bear examination either. It happens that the grade, the type of construction and everything else differs very little, and there is practically no

difference in regard to the specifications. If hon. members would care to go further into the matter they might examine the conditions which attended the construction of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway, making allowance for the infinitely different type of construction required because of the bush and muskeg country. I believe it will be found that the Canadian Pacific cost of construction, which showed a decline over a period of years, was closer to the mark than the cost of construction on the Canadian National.
I do hope the minister will take this matter into consideration, if only from the point of view of the rank and1 file of the men, who know these facts and who know that after all the technical experts, who are supposed to know so much, have been responsible for the appalling excess cost of Canadian National construction, amounting to over 830,073,000. That sum has been thrown into the sink by an over-staffed engineering department, apparently filled with its own authority and sense of power. The men responsible for that condition of affairs are retained in their jobs, and that is the point I want the minister to appreciate. I want to ask him to use his good offices to see that the men who have been responsible for these conditions are dealt with properly, and in the meantime I propose to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps).

nothing by way of protection for the employees. It is true that a couple of slight amendments were made in that chamber but I think it has transpired from the discussion in this house that in the main the employees were not protected as they should be. After a considerable controversy in this house, amounting almost to a fight, a few amendments in the interests of the employees were adopted, but in my estimation these amendments do not go nearly as far as the men expected the government would go. For instance, subsection 3 of section 16 contains a very indefinite statement. I ask the minister to follow me while I read this subsection. It reads :
The National company and the Pacific company for and on behalf as aforesaid are directed to endeavour to provide that any new company, created as in subsection two of this section referred to, shall give preference for work to employees in any services or on any works taken over by such new company.
Surely the words "to endeavour" have no place in that subsection. I have an amendment to refer this bill back to committee which I will send over for the minister's consideration. It is quite evident that at this stage any suggestion coming from this side of the house will not be considered very closely. I submit in all earnestness that the words "to endeavour" have no place in this subsection and I suggest that they be struck out before the bill finally passes. The amendment moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) covering compensation has been ruled out of order, and the amendment which I proposed to compensate employees for property losses due to economic measures which might be adopted was refused. It is true that the minister has stated that if section 2 of the bill was found to work out unjustly to the men, an amendment would be considered at a future session, but the section as it now stands does not go nearly far enough. An amendment moved by the leader of the opposition to provide that one of the trustees shall be a representative of the employees was also refused. The board of trustees is now surrounded by all safeguards possible and it is entrenched in a position where it can do almost anything with the road and, in my opinion, almost anything with the employees. It is only fair that one of the trustees should be a representative of the employees. The minister has said that the door was not closed, and I am living in hopes that the government may yet decide to appoint a representative of the employees as a member of this board of trustees. maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: What was the gist of the petition? It was against amalgamation, was it not?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
It was against amalgamation, yes, and the number of unemployed this measure would create. It is true that the petition was against amalgamation, but it added that this bill would create quite a number of unemployed, and also, in the last paragraph, it says:
It would not eliminate the tax burden of the citizens of Canada. The Canadian National Railways as shown in the Duff report, had an earning power from 1923 to 1931 inclusive, of $281,211,847 in excess of its operating expenses, but cannot take care of the interest on borrowed money. This bond indebtedness would not be taken over by the privately owned railway, but would still be chargeable to the people of Canada and paid for by them through taxation. Therefore, we maintain, it is far more desirable and businesslike to operate the Canadian National Railways in its entirety, and permit



C.N.R.-C.P.R.-Mr. Heenan
it to earn its operating expenses rather than sacrifice its most productive parts to a privately owned railway and still retain, for the taxpayers of Canada, the debt of borrowed money and the disastrous and far-reaching results of further unemployment of such gigantic proportions.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Of course that petition
has been complied with in the bill.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
The minister says so. I
am sorry I have to disagree with him.
Then we have resolutions from the town of Kenora, the town of Sioux Lookout, from Hornepayne, Nakina and Port Arthur, and from many organizations. Many of these have asked that the bill be left over for at least a year, so that the government might make a survey and take into consideration what the railroad companies, or the government which in the long run is responsible, propose to do with the number of railway men who will be discharged under this measure.
I also consider that this legislation is a breach of faith with the electors of Canada, and manifestly so, because the present government, the Prime Minister and his followers, promised from one end of the country to the other that there would be amalgamation never and competition ever. The minister says that this is provided in the bill. This is, to my mind, merely a very pious wish, but in order to satisfy the opposition there was incorporated in the measure part IV, section 27:
Nothing in this act shall be deemed to authorize the amalgamation of any railway company which is comprised in National railways with any company which is compromised in Pacific railways nor to authorize the unified management and control of the railway system which forms part of National railways with the railway system which forms part of the Pacific railways.
That, I think, is what the minister alluded to a few moments ago. But my contention is, that notwithstanding that, section 16 of the bill and the authority given to the trustees under it, practically amalgamates the operations of the railroads of Canada; giving the trustees power to form:
New companies controlled by stock ownership, equitably apportioned between the companies.
What is that but amalgamation? It gives them power to grant:
Leases, entrusting agreements, or licences, or agreements for the pooling and division of earnings arising from the joint operation of any part or parts of freight or passenger traffic, or express, telegraph, or other operating activities or services;
Joint trackage, running rights, joint ownership, or joint operating agreements, depending upon the nature of the property-

And so forth. What provision can be put into the law stating that there will be no amalgamation when there is right in that section a direction to the trustees that they shall amalgamate these services? I have been advised-I have not seen this-that the railroad companies are now selling joint tickets and they have their time cards arranged for consolidation of train services. What is the difference between calling it amalgamation, consolidation or cooperation? So far as the practical working out of the railways is concerned, the terms all mean the same thing. While it is true that section 27, which I read a little while ago, provides that the trustees can make no amalgamation of the finances of the companies and so on, yet the practical working out of the bill is an amalgamation of the railways. But even at that, it is a breach of faith because the present Prime Minister, when he was leader of the opposition, not only promised amalgamation never but said: Competition ever. This is just the opposite of competition; we are practically eliminating competition and in its elimination we are sacrificing, as I have said, between 20,000 and
40,000	employees. I am still of the opinion that by this measure at least 20.000 good citizens of Canada will be thrown out of employment. We are sacrificing them without any consideration as to what we propose to do for the future of those people or their families and other dependents. We are sacrificing them for what purpose? In the interests, as I have said before, of the money lenders of New York. We are throwing out from their employment between 20,000 and 40,000 Canadian citizens, men who were encouraged to enter railway service many years ago, and we are doing so to pay the money lenders of New York. When the time comes to take sides in this parliament, so long as I have a seat in this chamber I am going to take the side of and vote for the labour men of this country, our own good citizens, rather than taking the side of the money-lenders of New York and other parts of the world so that they get their last pound of flesh.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit a question? Would he mind offering to the committee some method by which we can get rid of the obligation of paying interest to what he terms the money-lenders, whether in New York or Canada or England?

speechtext:
I thought I had done that before, Mr. Speaker, but now that the minister has asked the question, and in the hope that he is really desirous of getting my opinion I shall give it to him. These are days of

CJ'f.R.-C.P.R.-Mr. Woodsworth
world depression. No one will deny that now. The only people who did deny it were the Conservative party in 1930, when they said it was a Canadian depression and that if they were elected they would remedy conditions within a very short time. But not even the members of the government will deny to-day that these are days of a world depression, days when every person is called upon to make sacrifices. The Canadian railroad men through the economies to be effected by this measure are called upon to make sacrifices, and for what purpose? So that we can pay the interest on our bonded indebtedness. Now is it not feasible and is it not right that we should tell the money-lenders of New York- I would do it whether it is right or wrong if the minister wants to know-that during this time of depression and until it has rolled by they could not get their interest?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Which, of course, is repudiation of our debt.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
I would not care whether you called it repudiation of our debt or not. Do we not also owe the citizens of Canada some debt? Have we not indebtedness to the workingmen of this country, to provide them with proper safeguards? When you talk of repudiation, must we always see that there is no repudiation of our indebtedness to the men who are lending the money, while at the same time we repudiate our debt to our returned soldiers who went overseas and fought for this empire and came back to their old positions on the railroads, and many of whom are going to be discharged under this bill? They have not got seniority enough to ensure them being kept on, and they are now going to be thrown off, many of them without a war pension because some of them were not injured and others did not ask for a pension. They are to be thrown into the discard so that some foreigner who loaned a million dollars to the Canadian National Railways will receive his last ounce of flesh. Yes, repudiate if you will, and when it comes to the time when I have to decide whether I am going to repudiate our debt to the man who has millions or repudiate our debt to the man who has nothing, I am going to keep faith with the workingman who has helped to build up these roads to the condition they are in to-day. When the minister talks about repudiation, why does he not think of the promise given to the railroad men in 1930? The promise to end unemployment, the promise that those engines that were standing idle on the side tracks near the roundhouse 53719-299J
would soon be belching forth smoke again and hauling commodities back and forth across this country, creating employment for Canadian railroad men at higher wages than were prevailing at that time. Are we not repudiating our word of honour to these people who voted for the government on the assurance that they would get consideration? This bill is the repudiation of everything that was promised to the electors of Canada. It means just the opposite of competition. It is amalgamation in the operation of the railroads of Canada. It will create unemployment instead of ending it. There is no provision made to take care of the men who will be thrown off, no provision for financial compensation of any kind. It is simply a case of breaking faith with the railroad men of this country, and I have no apology to make for saying that I am going to vote against the third reading of this bill, and that if I had a hundred votes they would all go against its third reading.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL

Mr. Speaker, I should like
to have it very clearly understood that we in this comer are not opposed to public ownership of the railroads, which ultimately will involve amalgamation. We believe in public ownership, but we believe in a genuine public ownership, and not in a public ownership which gives control very largely if not entirely to the financial interests, and which permits a private road to run in competition with the public road, and very often, it seems to us, throws the advantages to the privately owned road. We think the time is coming when in this country we shall have to have complete public ownership of our roads involving amalgamation at least, and including probably under one transportation commission not only the railroads but the motor transportation services and possibly the air transportation services.
At the present time we are not opposed to all economies which may be brought forward. We think that it is inevitable that some economies should be made, but according to this bill the economies are to be made in the interests of the bondholders. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) has denied that, but not very successfully; I do not think he was on good ground. It is undoubted that under the present set-up the bondholders are in danger of losing and because the Dominion government has to pay the deficits on the road the Canadian public is under the necessity of carrying a very heavy load. Economies should be effected if possible, but what we claim is that the rights of the individuals
4732	COMMONS
C.N.R.-C .P.R.-Mr. Woodsworth
who have helped to build up this system, the employees of the railways, should not be neglected. I think the position which we take is a sound one.
We would say that the care of the people who are thrown out of work by means of the economies under this bill should be a first charge on the savings effected. The minister tries to evade that by saying that there will not be a great many men thrown out of work. Well, I think everyone will recognize that the payroll of the employees is one of the largest items of railway expenditure, and if we are to have economy which will amount to anything it must be made as a result of laying off a very considerable number of men. That must be in contemplation. I quoted Mr. Beatty to that effect on one occasion, and I think his opinion still stands and is reasonable.
Further, the minister says that we ought not to make this provision ahead of time- wait until we see that men are thrown out of work, and how many will be thrown out. I do not think that is the way in which legislation should be put through the house. When the avowed purpose is to effect economies which can be made only through throwing people out of work, the time to safeguard these people is not at the next session of parliament, but now.
A good deal has been said in recent yeans with regard to the interference by government in business. I think we -may as well frankly face the fact that the whole of our railway enterprise is decidedly what might be termed an interference by government in business. The Canadian Pacific railway would not -have been built in the first instance had it not received very large subsidies from the public. Later on the Canadian Pacific railway and other roads that were constructed were able to -maintain their freight rates because of legislation passed by this house and by decisions of the Board of Railway Commissdonens. It was the failure of private ownership, as we all know, that -brought the Canadian National railway into being. There is a constant "interference" in business by the government, if you like to put it that way. The fact is that this interference has been pressed upon parliament and the public by the roads affected. I believe the evidence is clear that the present bill based on the Duff report is the result of pressure from the roads. In fact we were told by the minister that Mr. Beatty had suggested a commission should be appointed to consider the whole matter. So that if parliament is taking action at this time it is upon the request of the railways. There is no question of the government simply interfering
LMr. Woodsworth.]
in private affairs without any proper reason for so doing. In effect the railways have come and said, "You arrange matters so that we can make these savings possible; arrange -matters so that the bondholders will be protected." At this time we cannot lightly relieve ourselves of responsibility for the people this legislation will affect. We have given instance after instance of what is happening in poolings which have already taken place, of people who because of this legislation and arrangements for economy have already lost equities in their homes, people who because of having been transferred are to-day out of jobs, people who are too old to hope under present conditions to find new jobs. I urge these men have certain claims upon the Canadian National Railways and upon the government. For that reason my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) sought by his amendment to place this question fairly before the house. I think we have a right to do so. Mr. Speaker, at the risk of being charged by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), as he charged the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) with speaking for propaganda purposes, I intend to make a few remarks at this time, the last opportunity of speaking on this bill before it becomes law. I have in my hand a copy of the Canadian Unionist which came to me this morning. It contains the full speech of the hon. member for Kenora taken from Hansard, upon the second reading of the railway bill I have never seen reported in any press on this continent any such full and favourably reported speech of my own since coming to this house. That is how the speech of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, with his photo attached, has been referred to in this labour paper. I have only been able hurriedly to review this speech, but I believe it speaks not only for the railway men and the people of this country but for the Liberal party a3 well. That is all I can say with regard to the rather measly accusation made by the hon. member for Sunbury and some place else.
I am going to oppose the third reading of this bill although it is a much better bill than

C.NJt.-CPJt.-Mr. Motherwell
it was when it first started on its jaunt through parliament. As we know, it was originally defined by the Duff commission. It then went through the fanning mill of the upper house. It did not receive a very thorough screening there, the screens were too large and they let a lot of objectionable stuff through. It was given another fanning in the Commons. This was a more thorough fanning machine, it got out more dross and screenings but there is Still some vicious stuff and refuse left in. I want to get after that.
There is one objection, sufficiently important as I see it to condemn the bill to perdition forever, which can be made to this legislation. I refer to the abdication by the government of any safety control over the Hudson Bay railway. After this bill becomes law, the Hudson Bay railway can be taken over by these twin railway boards. The day after that it can be dismantled by the same twin boards. No restraining hand can be held out by this government to prevent this action.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
The Hudson Bay railway
does not come under this bill at all.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Oh, no, but it can
be brought under. That is a very nice interjection but unfortunately I am on my feet yet and I can puncture it right away. The Hudson Bay railway can be taken over at any time by this trustee board which has no railway president thereon. The national railways is still headless, as far as having a president is concerned. This trustee board has even more authority than the old presidency. It can take over that railway to-day and dismantle it to-morrow. Someone may say:	even though the government has
abdicated all authority over this great national railway which is the property of the men, women and sons of Canada, it will use a restraining influence upon any possible depredations by these twin boards. If it exerts any influence at all, what kind will it be? This government decapitated the railway by retiring Sir Henry Thornton; having done that, do you think it will refrain from doing less in connection with the remaining body of this headless railway? Certainly not. We know a tree by its fruits, and the fruits of this government, as far as the national railway is concerned, have been such as will turn sour in the mouths of the people of Canada who believe in the future of this railway. How can I back up that statement? I do it by referring to the penchant this government party has had for destroying this Hudson Bay railway as well as the National. It attempted to send this
railway to Port Nelson when every engineer in Canada knew that that port was a useless and hopeless outlet or inlet for the citizens of western Canada. If the road had been sent there it would have been ruined, and I invite anyone to challenge that statement. I invite any hon. member, including the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) to challenge that statement. If I attempt to read anything by way of proof the chances are the members of the press gallery will take a hike for their other rear quarters; they do not like to hear anyone reading anything. However, I may be obliged to read something if challenged but I will be prepared for their immediate exit. Perhaps I had better keep this opportunity and proof for another day. " He who fights and runs away will live to fight another day," if no one accepts his challenge now. It will be a fine thing for a subsequent occasion, and I have the dope to prove my statement. I have more to say but they cannot bear it.
There is very little use going over the past. I made only one note for my speech, and I made that on the back of this precious bill. That was the word "Pilate," not "pilot." Our hon. friends in the government have been the modern political Pilates in their attitude towards this national railway. They have washed their hands of this fine property of ours, they have abdicated their power over this railway and have handed it over to Herod. Both the original Pilate and Herod were afraid to do what in their hearts they desired to do. They had no Duff commission or Senate to which to pass the buck in those remote days.

speechtext: They had the sanhedrim.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: The action of the original Pilate and Herod finally resulted in the crucifixion which was ordained from the beginning of the world. These modern Pilates and Herods have been afraid like the originals to do what they would have liked to do. They took off the head of Sir Henry Thornton but they did not know how to mutilate the body sufficiently so that it would not be restored to life. The government have passed the buck to the national railway board and a tragedy is about to be enacted. As I see it, though parabolic this is mighty true to life.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of attention to my hon. friend. We have campaigned together for more than forty years in western Canada and his speech to-day is the same old red country schoolhouse one that he used to deliver most effectively in the west, all the time misleading the struggling masses on the western prairies. Representing as I do the most outstanding agricultural constituency in western Canada, what do I care what is done with the railroads as regards cooperation or anything else so long as we are given cheaper freight rates so that we may get the products of the land to the markets of the world? During all the years the hon. gentleman sat on the government benches there was not a single reduction in freight rates, either by sea or land; nothing but higher and higher ocean and land rates. No man can farm in western Canada under the conditions to which he is subjected to-day.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Yes, but this is the result of the actions of hon. gentlemen who occupied government benches during the last eight or ten years. Let me for a moment draw the attention of the house to the Petersen commission. What a fiasco it was! I was brought as a witness from western Canada to try to get a reduction in freight rates. With what result? Nothing at all, not one iota of reduction. Forty years ago in western Canada we had lower freight rates than we have to-day. When the Canadian Pacific was the only railway operating in the west, freight rates were 40 per cent less than they are today. But hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were in power, gradually raised and raised the rates until now they are prohibitive for the farmer who wants to deliver his products to the markets of the world. How insincere hon. gentlemen opposite are! This is impressed upon me when I think of one gentleman who made a speech in Montreal in reference to the Hudson Bay railway and of my hon. friend opposite who a few minutes ago talked so kindly of that railway. What did the gentleman say in talking to an audience in Montreal? Let me read this:
The Conservatives adopt a different attitude. The finances are upside down, yet they spend
FMr. Motherwell.]
millions on projects which can wait a year or two years, or even five years, without harming the stability of the country. What is happening to-day as regards Port Churchill? We have Hon. Doctor Manion acting like a beggar in the street, begging people to ship some grain over the Hudson Bay railway to Port Churchill.
That is the kind of speech hon. gentlemen opposite make when they get down to Montreal; then when they" come into the House of Commons they talk differently for the benefit of the man out west.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) assumes to speak on behalf of labour. I have ridden the freight trains in the pioneer days of western Canada and I have associated with those railway men. Far be it from me to do anything that would be detrimental to the men who operate the road. I was travelling over the Canadian Pacific when the line was coupled up at Jackfish many years ago. I know the hardships endured by the men who pioneered in those days. To-day the answer of the railroads as to why they do not give a lower rate, is: Look at the wages. The reason is not wages at all. In those days they had five of a crew and when we asked for fourteen cars for cattle, they gave us a trainload rate of sixty and a half cents a hundred from Winnipeg to Montreal. To-day we are paying eighty-five cents a hundred and the

C.N.R.-C.P.R.-Mr. Manion
crew of a train still numbers five; they are hauling five times the tonnage, seventy-five cars of cattle, with just five of a crew. So the reason is not wages. But when I look at the head officials, I think of Winnipeg with Sir William White, who came from the track up; I think of Robert Kerr, George Shaw and William Stitt. Their entire salaries did not amount to as much as one railway official is getting to-day in western Canada. It is the head officials who are getting the high salaries. Those salaries should be withdrawn so that the farmer out west may have some chance in shipping his products.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are insincere so far as the Hudson Bay railway is concerned, and if this government had not been in power, I do not believe we would have had the Hudson Bay railway to-day. In western Canada we have great hopes as regards that outlet; it can be developed and because of its coolness it is one of the best outlets for the live stock industry of the west. At times the port of Montreal is extremely hot, but up north we have good cool weather and the cattle will ship to the British market far better than they will out of ports down east. We want, however, all the outlets we can get; we want to be able to ship out of the country and at a lower freight rate.
I say to the railroads: I do not care what you do about cooperation or amalgamation but I do not want to see you build these luxurious trains between Toronto and Montreal and Toronto and Ottawa, trains de luxe for the creme de la creme of eastern Canada, while the man out west is struggling on side lines, sitting on ribbed seats so that when he gets up his back is like a washboard. That is the condition to which we are subjected on the branch lines in my constituency, but we are putting up with that. I want these luxurious trains withdrawn so that the man out west may have a chance to get back to conditions as they were in the pioneer days out west, when, over forty years ago freight rates were 40 per cent less than they are today. Under present conditions a man cannot carry on. The salary list on the Canadian National Railways-and there are some from t'he United States amongst the officials-is terrific; no farmer in a lifetime makes as much as these men were making in a year. These conditions will be righted by this government and through this cooperation. We say and I say:	Amalgamation never, competition ever. That will be carried out and by it I hope the commodities of western 'Canada, can reach the markets for which they are destined.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL-CAN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
I do not intend to delay the
house more than a few minutes. A number of hon. gentlemen have spoken and there are a few remarks I should like to make.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) took up the question of compensation for the men laid off. That question has already been dealt with very fully, and it has been pointed out, and I can only repeat, that when the time comes to look after all classes of men who are out of employment the railway men should be looked after at that time, but I do not believe that now is the time to pick out one particular class of men and give them compensation while other men, and even men in that same particular class, railway men who have been laid off previously, are not being taken care of.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) mentioned one item in the Duff report which so far as I know has not been mentioned before in the house, and that was the cost of branch lines. He touched upon a very important statement made by the Duff commission to the effect that the cost of branch lines in Canada on the Canadian National had been very much heavier than the cost on the Canadian Pacific, by the amount of some $30,000,000 in the last ten years. That was not overlooked by the government. I myself asked the Canadian National to give me an explanation of the difference in costs, and I hold in my hand a report which they gave to me some six or seven months ago, some time after the Duff report was tabled. They claim in that report that the branch lines went through different types of territory. It has been argued that that was Hot the case. I am not going to enter into a technical discussion of that kind, but I would point out to the hon. gentleman who stated that some of the officers now in charge of construction were the same as those who were in charge when the Duff report was made and during that construction period, that very heavy cuts have been made in the salaries of the officers higher up. For instance, a few of them who were drawing $30,000 are to-day receiving $18,000, or not much more than half of what they were getting. The engineer in charge of that construction work was not one of those getting that high salary, but he has been cut in proportion. After all it must be pointed out that the government has not the power and had not the power to dismiss any of these men, whatever officers they were. The government, through myself as minister, did draw tihe matter to the attention of the directors, and the directors and the present
C.N.R,-C.P.R.-Mr. Manion

management did bring about the economies which have been effected, and I submit that those economies were very marked and emphatically large. I pointed out in another address that I made in this 'house that apart from the wages for the men, with which we had nothing to do, the economies among the officers drawing over $3,000 amounted alone to something like $2,000,000 in 1932 as compared with 1930.
I do not think the hon. member for Bow River was quite fair in saying that there was a campaign against public ownership. Certainly there was not so far as the government was concerned. There was a campaign of education to tell the people of this country what it w'as necessary for them to know, the immense taxation which they had to pay to meet the deficits on the government roads. That is all that was done. So far as the government was concerned, there was certainly nothing at all in the Shape of a campaign against government ownership.
So far as the amendment of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) is concerned it seeks to amend the clause dealing with the creation of new companies reading as follows:
The National company and the Pacific company for and on behalf as aforesaid are directed to endeavour to provide that any new company, created as in subsection two of this section referred to, shall give preference for work to employees in any services or on any works taken over by such new company.'
The hon. gentleman proposes to wipe out the words "to endeavour." My legal officers advise me that so far as the companies can legally be forced to carry out this-shall I say-admonition to them they are forced to do so under this clause, and that to wipe out "to endeavour" would have no effect whatever. Therefore there is no reason for accepting the amendment. My hon. friend repeated not once, but many times, that no matter what we may say this bill is for the purposes of amalgamation. I can in reply only refer him to the last clause of the bill in which it is specifically stated that nothing in this act shall be deemed to authorize the amalgamation of the two companies. I do not wish to argue or harp upon that question any further.
I was satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) frankly came out in the open and said, particularly the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, that they believed we were looking after the moneylenders and ignoring the human element, and that we must repudiate our debts. I wish to point out in a sentence that the bonds of the

Canadian National Railways or rather the mortgages of the Canadian National Railways, because that is what the bonds of the Canadian National Railways guaranteed by the Canadian government are, are just as much the debts of this dominion as are the ordinary bonds which have been issued by the government of Canada at various times since confederation, and when the government of Canada takes the attitude that it will repudiate the payment of interest on the bonds of the government railways which it has guaranteed, then the government of Canada will have to take the position also of repudiating its ordinary debt, and I simply submit without further argument that that is the position taken by Russia, and Canada has not yet come to the position of repudiating its debts.
I would further point out to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and some other members on both sides of the house who have made a very strong argument in regard to the human element, that because we have not accepted everything they proposed, although we have accepted a great deal, does not in any way alter the fact that we are just as anxious to look after the men as is the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River or other hon. members of the house. But it is worth pointing out that the Canadian National Railways in January, February and March, and I think April of this year, has not covered its operating expenses, let alone paying interest on its debt to the public. That in itself shows the seriousness of the situation and the need for the economies which have been made. It also shows the difficulty of complying with every request that is made by some hon. member of the house.
I have two other points to make and then I will sit down. May I point out that the pooling arrangements which have taken place in connection with the services between Ottawa and Toronto, and Montreal and Toronto, were not brought about under this bill at all. Both the railways to-day, without this bill at all, have the right to go ahead and make the pooling arrangements which they have made, and those pooling arrangements had nothing whatever to do with this bill.
One last word about the speech of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), who said that we were in a position and implied that we would likely take advantage of it, to dismantle the Hudson Bay railway. I cannot quite understand why he should say that except for the obvious reason that he thinks it is pretty good political propaganda.

C.N.R.-C.P.R.-Mr. Donnelly

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO GIVE EXTRATERRITORIAL OPERATION TO ACTS OP PARLIAMENT

speechtext:
Hon. MAURICE DUPRE (Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 74, respecting extraterritorial operation of acts of the parliament of Canada.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sullivan in the chair.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO GIVE EXTRATERRITORIAL OPERATION TO ACTS OP PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
This question of extraterritoriality is of primary importance, and was dealt with by the Imperial conference of 1926. The problem was afterwards referred to the committee of experts, which later became merged in the conference on the operation of dominion legislation which met in 1929. That conference, after very careful examination of the whole question, recognized that in view of the state of uncertainty, and the differences in the dominion constitutions themselves, which were reflected in the legal opinion in these dominions, it was desirable that legislation should be passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom to make it very clear that the constitutional limitation did not exist. Accordingly a clause was recommended for inclusion in the statute of Westminster, and that action was approved by the Imperial conference of 1930. That clause is section 3 of the statute of Westminster, which is printed in the explanatory note to this bill, and reads as follows:
It is hereby declared and enacted that the parliament of a dominion has full power to make laws having extraterritorial operation.
As a result of this enactment, there can be no doubt that all legislation enacted by the parliament of Canada since December 11, 1931, which is the date on which the statute of Westminster came into force, has extraterritorial operation in all cases in which that intention of parliament has been clearly indicated. The statute however has no effect upon Canadian enactments prior to that date. There undoubtedly are on the statute books laws concerning which the question might be raised, giving rise to unnecessary litigation. The question arose with regard to the case of Dunphy v. Croft, which was based on

a seizure under chapter 16 of the statutes of 1928, which authorized the seizure of Canadian registered vessels hovering within the twelve mile limit. The Supreme Court of Canada decided that the legislation not coming within the provision of the statute of Westminster, by reason of having been enacted prior to the coming into force of that statute, was ultra vires of the parliament of Canada. This position was reversed by decision of the privy council in the same case, and the legislation was upheld in terms that justified the views expressed by the successive governments in this country throughout the period covering this controversy. Accordingly the enactment might fairly be regarded as a sort of declaratory enactment, and can be justified as placing beyond controversy the validity of Canadian legislation. Its object is to settle definitely this controversial question and prevent unnecessary litigation.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO GIVE EXTRATERRITORIAL OPERATION TO ACTS OP PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I am pleased to support this bill. I have always been of the opinion that this parliament had the right of extraterritorial jurisdiction in its legislation, but the decisions of the courts in the matter have varied in such a way that possibly it is better to have this bill made law in order to remove any doubt. As the language of the statute of Westminster indicates, it is declaratory:
It is hereby declared and enacted that the parliament of a dominion has full power to make laws having extraterritorial operation.
It was not a statute giving power but rather to declare that parliament has that power. However it is better, as my hon. friend has said, that there should be no doubt as to past legislation, and this bill should be made law.
Section agreed to, bill reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to provide that the advertising portion of newspapers and periodicals transmitted for a greater distance than forty miles from their place of publication, or of which the publication is of greater frequency than once a week, shall be subject to postage of two cents a pound where the space devoted to advertisements exceeds 20 per cent but does not exceed 30 per cent of the total space; of 3 cents a pound where such space exceeds 30 per cent but does not exceed 50 per cent; and of 4 cents a pound where such space exceeds 50 per cent.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bury in the chair.

Post Office Act-Newspaper Postage

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
This resolution was
placed on the order paper in my name by accident and so I am proceeding with it.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: Not by accident.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: It was an accident. There was no name on it and I initialed it. I am going to say something about it in a moment and make it very simple.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: The Postmaster General should be in charge of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: So he should.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: I suggest that the Postmaster General should be here to listen at least to his chief's argument on the bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
This resolution is very
simple. After the representations that .were made on behalf of those who where interested were heard, it was decided that only the latter part of the resolution would be proceeded with, so that it will read:
That it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act to provide that the advertising portion of newspapers and periodicals transmitted for a greater distance than forty miles from their place of publication, or of which the publication is of greater frequency than once a week, shall be subject to postage of four cents a pound where the space devoted to advertisements exceeds 50 per cent.
That is all; it is to meet a situation in which the Post Office Department has been cumbered and bothered with handling newspapers containing sixteen to eighteen pages of purely advertising matter, taking the place, in many instances, of catalogues. The Post Office authorities advise that the loss in handling newspapers in this country last year through the post was somewhere between $5,090,000 and $6,000,000. It would be impossible under existing conditions to correct the Whole of that loss, but in so far as it may be possible to dispense with the handling by the Post Office Department of very heavy papers containing from sixteen to eighteen pages of advertising, it is proposed to do so by charging four cents a pound for such handling. The matter really resolves itself into the handling of catalogues through sixteen to eighteen page issues of newspapers.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister explain the representations which led to the dropping of the other portions of the resolution?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
It was established beyond question that under existing economic conditions the newspapers were operating at a loss unless their advertising content was equal to 50 per cent. Newspaper representatives
53719-300 j
waited on the government and made a very clear statement showing the facts in connection with existing conditions. The really determining factor was the placing of the sales tax upon newsprint, a tax which had not been previously imposed. The result is that the revenue derived from that source will be equal to, if not exceeded by the revenue that might be derived from this.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: What is the estimated additional revenue under this postage?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
The officials of the
department say that it will be difficult to estimate what the additional revenue will be, because it is believed that the probable result will be that people will resort again to the use of catalogues rather than the utilization of newspapers, but if the same quantity were carried, the additional revenue would be in the vicinity of $100,000.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS

speechtext:
I did not ask for the
figure, after the representations that were made, and after it was decided to impose a sales tax on newsprint.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
Will this
afford protection to Canadian newspapers as against papers coming from the United States?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
There is already in that regard a tax which is not changed. The bill has not yet been distributed, but the explanatory note says that there is no change with respect to that. It says:
The effect of the proviso will be as follows:
(A)	Free circulation, no change.
(B)	Newspapers and periodicals when the space devoted to advertisements does not exceed 20 per centum, no change.
And so on up to 50 per cent, there is no change. After that the rate is four cents. Up to 50 per cent the existing rates, which were increased, as it will be remembered two years ago will still be continued; that is, they will be one cent or one and one-half cent as heretofore, but after 50 per cent, the rate will be four cents.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
Many United States newspapers contain a large number of pages of advertising. I was wondering whether the effect of this particular legislation would be to prevent to any extent the importation of United States publications.

Postage
Post Office Act-Newspaper

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: I should not think there are any United States newspapers with over 50 per cent advertising content coming into this country.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: Magazines.

indicate from the representations that the delegation made to him what the advertising content of the average country newspaper would be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: This, as will be observed, does not touch the ordinary country newspaper; it touches only the daily newspaper. The daily newspapers have an association and its representatives produced figures to show that under present abnormal conditions a newspaper could not be said to be profitable until its advertising content approximated 50 per cent. But under existing conditions it will be remembered that the newspapers, except in a few instances, do not carry such advertisements daily; they sometimes carry them once or twice a week for a page or two and then for the remaining days a smaller portion of space is taken. The old rule, I was told, used to be-and I asked that question-that 40 per cent advertising and 60 per cent news was profitable. Under present conditions, with the taxes such as they are, this rate had risen to practically fifty-fifty.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: Would this affect, for example, the Saturday Evening Post from Philadelphia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: That was covered by the legislation passed two years ago.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: It is not affected by this?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: My understanding was that none of that class of papers was affected. The section as it reads is section one as amended in 1931 and, as I say, there was no change made in that except the one I have just indicated. I shall, however, make inquiry and ascertain between now and to-morrow whether it makes any difference in the postage payable by that paper.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
It seems to me that if this legislation goes through, the newspapers will sit down and figure whether it will be cheaper to pay four cents extra postage or to increase the reading matter so as to bring the paper

under the lower postage rate. In this way the department may find itself in the position of carrying an increased weight without an increased remuneration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: I do not think that difficulty will arise.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: Is any change made in regard to the printed matter coming by express into Canada? If you go down street on Sunday morning in Montreal or anywhere else, you will see truck loads piled with United States papers that formerly would have gone through the mails.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext: They pay some contribution to the revenues of the country, although the exact basis I do not carry in my mind. It was discussed in 1931. There is no method at the present moment by which we can prevent Canadian newspapers from circulating their issues by trucks; in fact in the country in which I live, in western Canada, and I suppose it is so in many other parts of the country, newspapers are now distributed by motor trucks where the postal service is not quite convenient in view of the hour of publication. I believe that the magazines and newspapers that come into this country pay customs duties at the border, and distribution is a matter which is arranged between them and their distributing agents. They come in usually by express to large cities like Montreal and Toronto where there is a substantial Sunday distribution, but not in the case of the smaller communities.

maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS
speechtext:
Did not the
Prime Minister suggest that he wished to amend the resolution?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: NEWSPAPER POSTAGE BASED ON SPACE OCCUPIED BY ADVERTISEMENTS

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Tariff Board Act, chapter 55 of the statutes of 1931, to provide that the salary of the chairman shall be $15,009 per annum; and that any member of the board who has served for a period of ten years, and is, on completion of such period, of the age of sixty years or over, may be granted an annuity equal to one-half of the annual salary of such member.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee, Mr. Gagnon in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The purpose of this
resolution is to provide that the chairman of the board, who was a member of the high court of justice of the province of Ontario and who left that position to accept the position of chairman of the board, shall be placed in substantially the same position financially as he was had he not done so. The chairman did not seek the office; the office sought the chairman. I need hardly say to this committee that the appointment of a chairman to this board was a matter of
Tariff Board Act

very great difficulty. To secure one with judicial qualities of mind, and who would commend himself to all those who were concerned in the matters with which he had to deal was not the easiest matter in the world. I consulted in many quarters as to where a judge might be obtained because I believed it was desirable that the chairman should be one who had judicial qualifications.
Mr. Justice Sedgewick was not disposed to accept the position; he took some time to consider it. After consulting with some of his friends he was finally prevailed upon by his sense of public service and duty to accept the position. He was appointed judge in December of 1930, and had been on the bench something over two years. He is now of the age of fifty-five years, and was something over fifty-three at the time of his appointment to the bench. After taking some time to consider the matter he finally concluded, as an act of public service, to accept the position. He desired however that his financial position should not be worse than it would have been had he remained on the bench. This resolution is an endeavour to give effect to that purpose.
I think perhaps the only amendment would be that of changing the word "sixty" to "sixty-four," because it is desired to have regard for the fifteen years of service that he would render if he were on the bench, to secure an annuity. Two of those years are now passed and do not count for anything. We would provide that if he serves ten years as chairman and has reached the age of sixty-four or over, he will receive the annuity mentioned in the resolution.
The resolution as it reads relates to the chairman of the tariff board, irrespective of who he may be?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The Prime Minister's remarks had reference to the present chairman, Mr. Justice Sedgewick. Probably the resolution should not be limited in its application in the first place to the individual mentioned. However, other and quite different circumstances may arise on obtaining a successor.

I put it this way: Any
person who occupies a position of judge of the high court of justice of Ontario, who has his home and is established in the city of Toronto and who under ordinary circumstances, if his health is good, would be entitled to keep that position until he had reached the age of seventy-five years, and to retire upon an annuity of two-thirds of his salary, with a likelihood of promotion, so far as he was concerned, on the bench, would not be as well off financially by accepting the chairmanship, as if he had remained in his former position. That view was supported by business men whom he consulted, and with whom he discussed the matter as to whether or not he would be wise in making a change at this particular time in his life. Nothing but a desire for fairness to himself and his family induced him to accept it under conditions such as indicated in the resolution.

Tariff Board Act

I cannot agree with my
right hon. friend. Mr. Justice Sedgewick drew a salary of $9,000 from the dominion, and $1,000 from the province of Ontario. He could not retire and be superannuated, except for cause, illness or inability to fulfil his duties of office. That superannuation would have been at the rate of two-thirds of his salary as a judge, or $6,000 per year. Under the resolution before us there is provision for a salary of $15,000 a year. Then after ten years, even though he be only sixty-two or sixty-three years of age-[DOT]
