speechtext: No.

-he would be entitled to one-half of his salary, namely $7,500. It certainly is an improvement in his position. I desire to discuss this matter briefly irrespective of who is to be the incumbent of the position. I have no doubt that the present chairman is well qualified and may be a very good chairman of the tariff board, but I desire to protest against the practice which seems to have established itself in recent years, namely that of taking a judge from one of the high courts, placing him on some board and giving him a salary much higher than that received by the chief justice of the high court of the province from which he came, or judges of the appeal courts. It is a salary even higher than that received by judges of the supreme court of Canada. I do not believe that a man occupying the position of chairman of the tariff board must have better qualifications than one occupying the position of chief justice of the province of Ontario, or a justice of the supreme court of Canada. I do not think it is fair to the other members of the judiciary. Also I object to it on another ground. I do not think it makes for the respect which is owing to the bench that judges should appear as aspirants to these new positions being created in the way of tariff board, railway board, radio board and other similar boards, at higher salaries than their brothers on the bench. I desire to protest against this practice and I am opposed to this resolution.

For the same reason that the 'hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) has just stated I desire also to register my protest against this legislation. I find here according to section 8 of chapter 55 of the statutes of 1931 that pensions are provided for these people on the tariff board:
Every member who has served on the board for a period of at least ten years may be granted an annuity for the term of his natural life equal to one-fourth of the annual salary received by him during such period, and if he
has served for any period less than ten years but more than fire years, he may be granted an annuity equal to one-fifth of the annual salary received by him during such period.
Then subsection 2 states:
The chairman of the board shall be paid an annual salary of twelve thousand dollars, and the other two members shall each be paid an annual salary of ten thousand dollars.
And the secretary is to be paid $6,000. I think, Mr. Chairman, that the country will support our contention that at the time those salaries were fixed and these pensions provided we were dealing most fairly and even generously with the people sought for to serve in those high positions. I understand that Judge Sedgewick is a very prominent man, I have had occasion to meet him myself, and I would not say anything disparaging of him, but, being elevated to that high position, if this bill is passed he will receive a higher salary than any judge of the supreme court, higher than any judge in the land. I think in years past we have made a mistake in paying such big salaries as we have. For instance we increased the salary of the Auditor General from $9,000 to $15,000. I think it was a mistake. I think a judge of the court of appeal is entitled to a high salary, but if we now put the salary of this gentleman at $15,000 we are giving him as high a salary as the chief justice of the supreme court of Canada and the Prime Minister of Canada. We must not forget this, that the tariff board is only a fact-finding body, which moves only at the instance of the government, the Minister of Finance. They are not in the position of administering justice as judges sitting in any appellate court in Canada, who move because they are seized with cases that come before them from all parts of the land. This board is nothing more than a tool in the hands of the government. I think we are paying too much in increasing this salary to $15,000 a year. I want to register my protest most strongly, more especially in view of the fact that in all big business concerns at present it is the practice to reduce salaries as much as possible. And what did we see on the 30th of March last? This government which is asking us to-day to increase this salary to $15,000 passed an order in council at the instance of the Minister of Finance requesting all departments of the government to keep within bounds and seek to reduce expenses and not incur any expense unless absolutely necessary for the better administration of the country. I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he thinks i't is absolutely necessary that we should increase this salary $5,000-

000,000 when the prices for agricultural products were comparatively high, certainly much higher than they are at present and higher than prices are likely to be for some time to come, how much will it cost to collect the $63,753,000 outstanding? I think it
is unfair to both branches, because in turn each branch is blamed by critics of the other branch. For the sake of peace within the ranks of the settlers themselves it would be advisable to separate the items. Perhaps the department knows that the soldiers do not like to have these costs jumbled up in this way, so that no one knows whether or not the cost of administration in connection with soldier settlement is unnecessarily high. In my opinion that cost has been absurdly high; it has been out of all proportion to the service rendered. It seems perfectly ridiculous that it should cost $21,709,000 to collect $50,000,000. I think the items should be separated, even though it may cost a little more.

I am not prepared to take the position that the cost has not been high. Of course it has been too high; that was abundantly apparent to me in 1930. I could not understand why it should be so high, but, as the hon. member knows, that cost has been reduced by about half so that to-day the cost of administration is less than one per cent, which compares very favourably with the cost of administration of loan companies handling similar business. I hope it can be held at that ratio, and it may be possible to make the cost even lower.

$63,000,000. No one needs to labour the point with regard to the cost of administration. I do not say this in any endeavour to stir up political matters, but we found field supervisors who had driven the cars of the board across the continent on their holidays, and all that sort of thing; we found men employed by the board who were of absolutely no value. In the reorganization
the endeavour was to select from the officials those with actual experience in pioneer settlement and agricultural work, and a review of the personnel of the board at present will show that almost one hundred per cent of the employees are returned men. In almost every case the men in charge have had very considerable experience in agriculture as well.
The history of this effort is well known to every member of the committee. Whether or not it was a proper effort to be made at the time perhaps does not matter now in discussing the situation as we find it, but I believe there should be a constant reduction in the cost of administration. I do not know that I can promise that there will be a very great reduction in each succeeding year, but it should be reduced to the point where the staff will be able to take care of land settlement generally, and the administration of these lands will be practically incidental. I have a very high regard for those who are at present employed as officials of the board; I believe hon. members will agree that politics did not enter into the reorganization at all.

When this item was up before on March 30, some five or six weeks ago, the minister said that only the day before he had spent a couple of hours with the heads of the mining companies, both east and west, looking into the whole situation in the hope that a solution might be found, favourable to them, of course. Can the minister tell me if any such solution has been found?-because I have heard no word of it. I have the press reports under my hand, and they indicate that nothing was arrived at, and the report given out by the principal coal operator on his way home was to the same effect. I wonder if the minister can give us any definite information or hold out any prospect of any policy in the immediate future looking towards an increased bonus, or the imposition of dumping duties to keep out British coal, or possibly some measure of reciprocity with the United States, or whatever his policy is. If he has anything of the kind that will be of assistance to our coal mines, now running three days a fortnight in some oases, it will be very gratefully received.

During the last two and a half years I have had many conferences with the coal producers with respect to this most complex problem. Those who come from mining areas are well aware of the fact that in the last twelve years, so far as coal mining in Canada is concerned, the whole picture has been entirely reversed. Twelve years ago we had a consumers' problem; to-day it is a producers' problem.

It is still a consumers' problem. People do not know how to pay for their coal.
(Mr. Neill.]

Of course, I am speaking broadly, so far as the fuel situation of Canada is concerned. Many factors, some of which have been worldwide, have contributed to a contraction in the consumption of coal. If one cared to look at the figures for the United States, Great Britain, Germany, Poland or other large coal producing countries, he would find that in the consumption of coal Canada stands in quite a favoured position, although it is a fact that consumption has very considerably dropped off. Other substitute fuels have contributed to a reduction in consumption. We have had milder temperatures during the last two winter seasons, and this factor has contributed to the lack of production and consumption of coal in Canada. Railroads both here and in the United States have greatly reduced the amount of coal they consume. These factors, along with some others, have placed the coal miner in a most difficult position. As the hon. member for Weyburn probably would say, it may be better not to support the production of coal in Canada if such production cannot be justified on a strictly economic basis.

Hear, hear.
Mr.-GORDON: There are many arguments, however, in favour of the proposition that that viewpoint should not prevail. If we placed ourselves again in the position we occupied between 1918 and 1923, and were paying as high as $27 a ton for anthracite coal-as I have done-then the consumer would find that the efforts the previous government made, and which we have continued in a larger way, are giving the consumer a protection he never had before. The figures cannot be denied; they are plain and their effects are self-evident.
We were entirely at the mercy of one source of fuel, namely, Pennsylvania anthracite. To-day there are many competitive lines of fuel. It is the desire of this government and, I believe, of the members of the committee generally, that this or any other government should take such action as it can take, -by way of assisting the coal mining industry, which will permit the carrying on of that industry at least in the mines of Canada which are best able to carry on at a cost per ton which is reasonable and which reflects efficient mining effort. If one of the coal mining communities shuts down by reason of the closing of the coal mines, the people dependent upon the industry will find themselves in a very difficult position. Perhaps among all the various members of our population there are none so helpless as the coal miner, if I may put it that way, in turning to any other vocation. That has been the

Supply-Mines-Coal
history of coal mining since historical records of the industry have been kept. As I say, it is a difficult situation. The hon. member for Weyburn said he intended to express the views that the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth would have expressed.
Should express.

I thought the hon. member said "would". Had he said "would express", then I would say that the principle underlying this assistance was one of which the hon. 'member ,for Shielbume-Yarmouth was certainly an outstanding proponent and advocate. Holding the views that I do with respect to bonusing industries which cannot struggle along on their own feet, it is difficult at times to subscribe to the principle here involved. Yet, with respect to the coal mining industry of Canada I believe any government would be justified in giving such relief as would permit efficiently operated mines to continue. Because, as I said a few moments ago, if we close our coal mines in Canada and revert to the position we were in ten or fifteen years ago, when we were relying upon a source of supply from one country, the consumer will be back just where he was before and will have to pay the price demanded.
Or through the eastern combine.

Quite, the eastern-and
western-combine, if one cares to turn to those subjects. Whether or not there is a combine within the meaning of the act, in the east or in the west, has yet to be determined. Competition unquestionably reduces the price of coal to the consumers of Canada. I do not wish to labour this point. However, that is one of the problems with which this country has been and will always be confronted. It is a challenge to the wisdom of those who laid down the political boundaries of the country, and it is again an acknowledgement that the Infinite Being did not place nature's resources where we poor humans could take advantage of them with the least possible effort. It challenges the ingenuity of anybody to make the Canadian coal fields available to industrial centres. The government is doing the best it can. Conferences I have held with coal producers and consumers have not resulted in any solution of the problem.
No, they have not.

I am quite prepared to
admit that. I have not heard any suggestion from anyone that I consider would be a solution of the problem of keeping the coal mining industry on its feet and going. As I say, no solution has been arrived at; I doubt very much if there is any complete solution, because there is certainly a limit to the extent to which one can resort to the treasury for moneys to be devoted to such purposes. No doubt there is a limit. I trust the government will not exceed that limit but will at the same time give such assistance as in the eyes of the taxpayers of Canada will be justified.

Mr. Chairman, I really was
sorry-and I do not speak sarcastically-to hear the reply of the minister. If ever there was a case of asking for bread and getting a stone, it was this. His remarks, with which because of their obvious truth, we must all agree, would have been very suitable in giving a lecture to the Young Women's Christian Association, or something of that kind. But in dealing with a condition as vital and desperate as that which we have in the west,
I do submit his remarks were inadequate. Really, on my word of honour, I did hope that he had at least some hope for us in the west. He says he has no solution of the problem, and that no one has ever offered any.
I offered one just now.

Would any friend who is afflicted with fiscal fanaticism mind letting me handle this? I know he is unique in his own sphere, but we are dealing with the world of reality, hungry miners and starving women, and we cannot feed them with fiscal fanaticism. Now the minister says no one could present a solution. I am not here nor is it my business to present a solution for the whole of Canada; that is the minister's problem, but in some small measure I may be able to present a solution for the miners that I represent. I submit that there is a way by which the immediate troubles affecting the coal mines of Vancouver island at least may be relieved, namely by putting a dumping duty on British coal subsidized by the British government, brought out largely as ballast, and under conditions that call for dumping restrictions if ever such restrictions are justified.
I want to speak, now, for a moment, of another matter. When this vote was up before I called the attention of the minister, as will be found at page 3572 and following pages of Hansard, to the manner in which the coal problem had been dealt with in Great Britain. I pointed out that they had discovered or developed a new form of fuel known as colloidal fuel, a mixture of oil and coal dust,
Supply-Mines-Coal

which enabled coal dust to be used in a way that it had never been used before. They had some process that prevented the heavier particles from sinking, and it gave promise of creating an enormous demand for a very low grade of coal and to compete with fuel oil. I also pointed out, having got this information from the British press, that this process had been developed to the stage where the British admiralty, always a most conservative body-if you make a deal with the British admiralty you have got to show you have the goods and continuity of supply of that quality and price-had made a contract for twelve months with some local firm, I think, in England, for the supply of fuel developed from coal for use on one of the British warships, a destroyer calledi the Westminster. Since then I see they have also adapted it for use on aeroplanes. Everyone knows that aeroplane gasoline must be of the very best quality, and if the British have developed an oil from coal that can be used in aeroplanes it certainly points the way for us to follow as a means of solving the question of the use of this coal. The day has gone by when we can dig and sell it "as is," as run of mine. We have to put it in a form to meet the competition of fuel oil and other competing fuels. I suggested that the government might have put this information before the coal miners of Canada, and asked them if they had any bulletin of the kind. The minister replied:
Obviously the hon. member has not read the annual report of the mines branch, which deals at great length with the subject to which he has made reference. . . .
Naturally that coming from the minister was supposed to make me feel squashed by the dignity and weight of his authority, but, I could not remember anything of that kind' in the report. I thought perhaps I had missed it, so I looked it up. I have the report here. It consists of fifty pages, and when the minister said that the subject I referred to had been dealt with in the report, at great length, how many pages would you expect to be allotted, in a pamphlet of fifty pages, to a matter that was dealt with "at great length"? Would you say fifteen, twelve, ten, or what? Or would it be like the man who was striving to save the people of Sodom from the vengeance of Jehovah? Perhaps even one page would justify the expression "at great length": But what are the facts? There is no reference whatever to the term "colloidal fuel." Reference to low temperature carbonization occurs in two instances, one less than two lines, and the other two and a half lines; that does not deal with the matters I was speaking about, the practical use of this fuel to the extent 1
IMr. Neill.]
indicated on British warships. One is simply a casual reference, and the other merely a statement that scientific men had continued work on the development of the new F.R.L method for the low-temperature carbonization of coals. But the British people have gone far beyond that. I suggest that it was a wholly improper statement to make, that the subject had been dealt with' at great length, when the only reference thereto was as I have indicated.
This subject of colloidal fuel and the production from coal of gas or oil sufficiently fine to be used in British warships or aeroplanes belonging to the navy is certainly a subject of practical constructive importance, one to which it would well become us to pay the very closest attention with a view to stimulating its development in Canada. I do not believe that even my hon, friend from Weyburn would object to spending public money on developments along these lines, because it would be helping the coal industry to help themselves. Once turn run of mine coal into products such as these and a vast market is opened up, and perhaps the coal mines would not need government subventions thereafter. I am quite sure I would have the support of the hon. member for Weyburn in that regard. As I say, these are constructive ideas leading to permanent improvement of the industry, and it is in that respect I complained about the coal mines branch. I do not blame the minister wholly; he is only the head of it, but the coal mines department is slack in looking after these developments.
The minister also said, and I have no doubt he was correct, that the principal coal operator on Vancouver island had written to him that he regretted my taking this matter up, that he was getting along much better without my interference. A case of butting in! Well, I did keep out of the matter until patience and abstention ceased to be a virtue. I left it to the minister and to the coal operator on Vancouver island to adjust it. Coal was coming in last year and in the early months of this year to a dangerous extent, but I did nothing; I was waiting, partly to be asked to take the matter up and partly to give them an opportunity to get together, as he said he was doing, and find a solution. If I did butt in it was only when I was asked by a representative elected body from the coal mine that is in my district, and when I found that there was nothing doing. And what did I do then? Did I take any unlawful or improper action by way of butting in? I hardly think it. I took the regular line; I wrote to the minister under date of January 23, presenting the matter reasonably and temperately

Interest Act-Mr. Coote
to him, and the answer I got under date of January 31 was in part:
I cannot say at the moment just what steps may be contemplated to deal with the situation.
That was in January. Three months later, on March 29, the subject came up again and I did feel that I was justified in asking what if anything had been done or what was contemplated. The minister on that occasion said he had had a meeting just the day before. A week later I found in the press under a name known to be close to the government, an intimation that it was not anticipated that anything would come out of the negotiations, which was proved to be all too true by the statement the minister made this afternoon. Then I find that Colonel Villiers, the largest coal operator on Vancouver island, gave an interview in Winnipeg on his way home; he said the minister had expressed his views in the bouse, and that was all there was to it. He also remarked that he employed 2,000 men at present on a part time basis, and he stated:
They are fine, stout hearted fellows and deserve much credit for the fine way in which they are making the best of difficult times.
I entirely endorse that statement, but for the very reason that they are fine fellows and are making the best of present conditions it is more necessary than ever that the coal operators, the minister and the department exert themselves in an endeavour to find a solution to this very difficult problem. It is all very well to say they are fine men; that hardly meets the situation, which is getting worse. I have a letter here from a very prominent man in one of the coal mining towns on the island, a well known Conservative; he says that during the last fortnight in March the mine worked for three days. So I say matters are getting worse. I have before me the record of the coal output for March of this year. As compared with March of 1932 the coal output of Vancouver island dropped from 70,391 tons to 49,663 tons, a drop of 25 per cent. In view of this ever decreasing production on Vancouver island is it not time for me, even at the risk of being told that I am butting in and that I lack propriety and dignity, to stir up the dead ashes and try to find some solution, or at least get some action?
I have already suggested some steps that might be taken. Great Britain subsidizes her coal; the exchange is against us, and it is convenient to bring coal in ballast as a result of the conference agreements. These are all factors which enter into the situation, and I suggest that the time has arrived when we should apply those dumping duties that have
been so readily and quickly and gladly imposed by the Minister of National Revenue in matters affecting indutries in Ontario. They hardly need to wait a day to get that dumping duty slapped on. We have seen these dumping duties applied with such haste that they have had to be removed after two or three days because it was found that they did not meet the situation. Now I should like to deal with another matter, and perhaps at this time we might call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

attitude taken by the minister might be summed up in this way:	he sympathizes
with any person who has to pay interest rates of any size with commodity prices at the present levels, but he feels that nothing can be done about it. That is not quite correct.
I said that a percentage of the reserves of the insurance companies, to be decided by the minister, should be invested in these four per cent securities.

I accept the correction of the Prime Minister. I think he proposed a very proper practice when he suggested that a certain percentage of the reserves held by the banks and insurance companies should be in-

vested in that four per cent issue. I should like to read briefly from his proposal. He said:
Therefore I propose that the Minister of Finance should, after creating his four per cent consolidated Canadian securities, provide by legislation that a percentage, to be hereafter determined, of the revenue of the insurance companies, amounting to a net total of over $110,000,000 this year, and from the deposits of the Canadian people in our savings banks, amounting approximately to at least another billion and three-quarters, should be utilized for the purpose of paying off this $100,000,000. This four per cent security I would maintain at all times at par-a very simple process.
I think the Prime Minister made a very useful suggestion at that time, one which the government of that day might very well have acted upon. The Minister of Finance referred to the bonds of Alberta and British Columbia which he said were selling on a basis to return 6.6 and 6.45 per cent respectively. I want to say without any mental reservation that no province in Canada can afford to pay such rates of interest. It was current gossip at that time that the provinces were held up by the bond houses and told that if they would not accept the offer made at that time they would not be able to sell their bond issues at all. It is to be regretted that the Dominion government did not tell the money authorities at that time that they must take up those bond issues at a lower price. Either that, or the provinces should not have floated any issues. However, the provinces were helpless and they had to accept the bids made by the bond houses or do without.
I think it all comes back to the fact that in 1931 the Canadian government floated the national service loan at a price which returned over five per cent. When that loan was issued the price of all other bonds outstanding in Canada was depressed. Bond prices fell almost immediately afterwards. Practically every financial institution in Canada had millions invested in these bonds and the depressed prices had a serious effect upon their balance sheets. Later on in the year the government passed an order in council authorizing the banks and insurance companies to value their securities at higher prices than those at which they were quoted on the market. There would have been no need for that action had the government insisted that the national service loan be taken up at four per cent. Then the provinces could have easily financed their needs at five per cent. In 1927 the Prime Minister did not hesitate to say that he would insist upon the banks

Interest Act-Mr. Coote
and insurance companies investing a certain percentage of their reserves in the bond issue at four per cent, and I think he should have insisted upon the same thing in 1931. In 1931 commodity prices had fallen off by at least thirty per cent as compared with those prevailing in 1927. Yet every province in Canada has been compelled to pay interest rates much higher than they paid before.
The minister then went on to say that setting a maximum rate of interest would interfere with control of credit and interest in Canada by a central bank. I would say that when the minister establishes a central bank in this country he can repeal this legislation if it should have become law. Further than that, may I say I have asked for years that a central bank should be established. If we had had a central bank properly established and operated, the government would never have had to pay five per cent interest in times of low commodity prices. If we had had that central bank I would not be bringing in this bill to-night. But the question in my mind is: Is the government going to establish a central bank, and, if so, when is it going to be established? I have waited until practically the end of the session to bring in this bill. I hoped the government would take some action to raise commodity prices, to bring about lower interest rates. I hoped the banking committee might before this have recommended that some action be taken in regard to interest rates on existing obligations. But nothing happens; the committee does not report. The government does nothing; it does not establish a central bank or do anything to raise commodity price levels. Are we to sit here doing nothing and see our people left at the mercy of the money changers? Last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) said:
No agriculturist, no industrialist and no merchant can afford to pay ten per cent interest for the money he uses in his business; it simply cannot be done; normal business will not permit of that rate of interest. Moreover, no bank can afford to take a loan at ten per cent, because it is too risky.
Then again he said:
But I lay down the principle that a rate of interest around eight or ten per cent makes successful operation of the ordinary business activities impossible and unprofitable.
The Minister of Finance said the other night that old established industries in Canada are paying nine per cent. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said last year: They cannot do that. The Minister of Finance said that great public utilities with long records of good service behind them are paying ten per 53719-301
cent. Is it not time that we do something about this? The Minister of Trade and Commerce said last year that business cannot pay these rates and we know they cannot. Evidently something should be done about the matter, but the Minister of Finance does nothing. He says:
It is idle to suggest, even with all the "isms" that are afloat to-day, that there is any other method whereby the rate of interest can be determined than the age-old law of supply and demand.
Well, we could take some steps to increase the supply. In the last three yeare the supply has been lessened by $700,000,000 and this house has done nothing about the matter. If we would increase the supply by the $700,000,000 that has disappeared in the last three years, we would be doing something. If there is anything in the argument of the Minister of Finance that there is only so much money; that we must pay that rate of interest and that the rate is determined by the law of supply and demand, let us increase the supply; the demand, we will take it for granted, remains the same, and according to the minister's argument, the rate will come down. I think that naturally follows.
Let us look for a moment at what is being done in the United States. In a dispatch in the Ottawa Journal two or three days ago, I find this:
Inflation bill is passed by the United States house.
These are the chief provisions as listed in the press dispatch:
The president is authorized to arrange with the federal reserve banks and board for the banks to purchase in the open market up to $3,000,000,000 of government obligations, including stock in corporations of which the United States is the majority stockholder.
If the president is unable to arrange this operation, or if it be found inadequate to raise prices to the desired level, the president may.
Direct the issuance of United States notes up to $3,000,000,000 to buy government obligations, and make provisions for retiring four per cent of this amount annually through congressional appropriations.
If our government is prepared to take similar measures in Canada, it can reduce the rate of interest on all government obligations The president is also given power to:
Reduce the gold content of the American dollar by as much as 50 per cent.
Provide for the unlimited free coinage of silver at a fixed ratio with gold.
In addition, the president is authorized to accept silver up to $200,000,000 in payment of war debts during the next six months, valuing the silver up to fifty cents an ounce, to be used as the basis for the issuance of silver certificates.

Interest Act-Mr. Coote

I do not think our government can afford to sit back and say: We can do nothing about the matter. This government could very well take similar measures.
Does the hon. member's bill apply only in future, or does it apply to past due interest? I want to ask possibly three questions.

I intended to mention that
before I sat down. The bill applies only to future borrowings. The reason that I have not asked that it apply to existing obligations is that that matter was definitely referred to the banking and commerce committee and I did not like to go to the length of asking the house practically to take that matter out of the hands of the committee.
It was not made retroactive because of the fact that possibly legal opinion had arrived at the conclusion that past due interest was a matter of civil contract.

I would not like to answer the hon. member on that point; I am not a lawyer. I know there are conflicting opinions, but I understand that the majority of the opinions given to the committee by the authorities to whom they sent a questionnaire are to the effect that jurisdiction over interest on existing obligations also rests in the dominion house.

One more question. With reference to the future, I assume the hon. member will agree with the proposition that capital is fluid. Supposing we fix in this country an interest rate beyond which one cannot go and the interest rate in the country to the south becomes higher; will the money be loaned in Canada or will it be loaned in the United States or any other country where there is a higher interest rate than that in Canada? If that condition arose, what would the hon. member do to meet it?
The Prime Minister has very wide powers under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, and, if necessary, he could correct any situation which might arise such as the hon. member suggests.
Surely the hon. member, being a free trader, would not agree to the restriction of capital.
This is second reading, not committee of the whole house.

I am glad to have the hon. member's question and, sir, I do not object, so long as you will allow it, to any question which may be asked in regard to the bill which I have introduced. If the hon. member

will make a thorough study of this question of the movement of capital, he will find there is not in Canada very much capital that can be moved out. Most of the capital that is invested in this- country is invested in factories, plants, railroads and similar assets of one kind or another; there is not very must of what is generally referred to as liquid capital which can be moved out of the country.
In case a situation did arise where capital could profitably be invested outside of Canada, is the hon. member in favour of an embargo on capital in order to meet such a condition?
That is a situation which I do not think will arise, and I do not think at the moment-
Suppose it did arise.
I do not think it can.
But the banks to-day have hundreds of millions of dollars on deposit.

If the hon. member will allow me to put the matter in this way: Were I adviser to the Minister of Finance at any time and such a condition arose, I would say to him: Let those people take their capital out if they know any way of doing so and we will supply the deficiency by drawing on our national credit; we will replace that capital with national credit borrowed from our central bank. I think that is the best kind of capital we could have in Canada.
In other words, the hon. member would inflate our currency?

That would not be inflation; it would be reflation; it would be replacement of capital taken away with capital raised on our national credit. (That national credit would cost us nothing and we would get rid of capital that is costing us high rates of interest.
But there is the question of the currency that has gone out of the country.

If we can print any currency that will go out of the country and stay out we shall be that much to the good, but this currency has a habit of coming back to Canada just about two days after it gets out, and we have to redeem it. If we send out too much and it comes back to be redeemed, our dollar would soon be depreciated in outside countries. Then we would get a rise in the commodity price level which the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg himself will admit is badly needed.

Hear, hear.

Interest Act-Mr. Coole

So the more capital goes
out of Canada under those conditions the better for his constituents and mine.
I have perhaps dealt with this question a little longer than I had intended. Before I leave the position of the United States and the action that has been taken there, I want to draw to the attention of the house the effect which that action has already had in raising commodity price levels in the United States. These figures are taken from the New York Times which I saw in the library to-day. According to Moody's commodity price index in the United States, using the index figure of December, 1931, as 100, on March 31, 1933, which was five or six weeks ago, the index figure stood at 86.3, and on May 5 at 110, a rise of 24 points inside of six weeks. That shows what can be done by a man who is determined to get action. It is a result of the action of President Roosevelt of the United States, and I only wish that Canada had a Roosevelt in power here.
I have introduced this bill more particularly because of the position of mortgagors in Canada. Their mortgages are falling due, and as I said the other night, I have the proof in my files that mortgage holders are forcing people to pay a higher rate of interest now when they are renewing their mortgages. Mortgage companies have been paying dividends of 11J per cent for the past three years. Borrowers on mortgage cannot afford to pay any higher rate of interest now than they have paid in the last three years. Many of them find it almost impossible to pay interest at all, and why they are held up in this way when they have to renew their mortgages is more than they can understand. Because I cannot get action in any other way I finally came to the conclusion that I should introduce this bill. The United States congress has passed a bill to set aside a fund of two- billion dollars for the financing of farm mortgages, and any mortgage holder can go to the federal land bank in the United States and exchange his mortgage up to fifty per cent of the value of the property for bonds bearing interest at the rate of four per cent, which are guaranteed by the government of the United States. The mortgagor then pays to the land bank 4^ per cent, regardless of the rate stated in the original mortgage and this bill has been amended so that small home owners with mortgages on homes valued at $10,000 or less can get exactly the same advantage under the bill as farmers. Are we doing anything to assist mortgagors in Canada? I say frankly that this interest bill is not the 53719-301 i
kind of bill I would really like to introduce into this house, but everyone knows that the rules of the house prevent private members introducing any bill which calls for the expenditure of a dollar. So we are precluded from bringing in many bills which we should like to see enacted here. We have urged the government repeatedly to bring in a money bill of some kind which would give us a little inflation or reflation in Canada. We have asked them for that so often that I am not going to do it any more. We have also asked them to establish a central bank. We cannot bring in a bill for that purpose. I would also like to see established some kind of public finance corporation to make an advance of even fifty per cent against these farm mortgages as well as urban mortgages at a rate of perhaps 3^ or 4 per cent. But as I said, we cannot introduce such bills, and the government so far has refused to do anything at all along that line. As the rules will not allow me to introduce such a bill there is only one thing left for me to do, and that is to introduce this bill asking that a limitation be placed upon the rate of interest which can be legally charged in Canada. I have already said in answer to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg that I do not ask that this legislation be retroactive or apply to existing mortgages. That was referred to the banking committee.
There is, of course, some question as to whether or not this house has jurisdiction. In my humble opinion it has, but I do not pretend to know because I am not a lawyer. I think it is beyond doubt that we have the power to fix a maximum rate of interest for new obligations.
I admitted the other night that there might be a very proper objection taken to this bill in the case of small loans. I think we should allow a service charge to be made in the case of small loans, not because large loans are safer than small loans, for the majority of the losses which have been made in this country have been made on large loans. I think on the average the small loan is the safer, but sometimes the interest charge on a very small loan is so small that a service charge in addition is justified, and I said to the house that I would be very willing to have an amendment made to the bill providing for that if the bill were allowed to go into committee.
There may be another objection in the minds of many members, and that is in asking for a maximum rate of five per cent. I have set that rate in the bill after a good deal of thought. I finally felt that five per
Interest Act-Mr. Coote

cent was as high as people could afford to pay, and if we are going to fix it on that basis I think five per cent is about as high as we ought to go. I have heard some members say that they would agree to the bill if the rate were higher than five per cent. As far as I am concerned I would be glad to have the bill go into committee and let the committee decide what that rate ought to be, although I have set five per cent in the bill. If the house is willing to allow the bill to go into committee, perhaps the committee can agree on a higher rate that might be fixed as a maximum, and then the house can decide on the third reading whether the bill should be passed. But I certainly feel, seeing that we have not taken any action to raise commodity price levels or lower interest rates or make more money available, some action should be taken by this house for the protection particularly of those whose mortgages are falling due. There are many people, of course, with other money contracts, and these money contracts they are, in some cases, being forced to renew for a period of years at a higher rate of interest than in the old obligation. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I ask for the bill the most favourable consideration possible by this house.

At six o'clock I had not concluded my remarks on this item. This after noon I urged upon the minister to develop or announce a policy which would in some measure tend to rehabilitate the decadent
coal mining industry in British Columbia, and more particularly on Vancouver island. In reply to his request for some suggestions I made one or two which I shall briefly summarize under four headings. The first, and the one which I think holds best promise of a permanent solution of the difficulty, would be that of following the lead given by Great Britain along the line of development. If necessary, money should be spent, because money spent in that way would be used to better purpose than if it were spent for subventions. We would be enabled ultimately to be independent. The money would be spent in the development of methods of presenting the coal in what might be termed modern up to date forms. It could be processed in such ways as colloidal fuel oil, or as gas obtained from coal, so that it could compete with other fuels. As I indicated this afternoon, if such fuel could be used on government warships or government aeroplanes it would develop a great general demand. Secondly,-and this is only a temporary expedient-greater subventions should be granted in respect of the coal mined on Vancouver island. Such subventions should be in line with those granted to other areas in Canada. It is notorious that the subventions granted to Vancouver island are out of all proportion smaller than those granted to other coal areas in Canada. Third, I suggested that before the matter has gone too far, and before it has reached the status of an established industry with large sums invested, we should stop the development of trade with Great. Britain on coal imported into British Columbia under the advantages of subsidies, low exchange and use as ballast. My fourth suggestion was that we might negotiate some form of reciprocity with the United States in connection with coal trade. I made the same suggestion in the house last year regarding, coal and fish, but I did not receive much support from hon. gentlemen opposite. However, the idea seems more popular just now.
None of these suggestions is unreasonable, and if any of them would help they should be accepted. Half of them would, I believe, put the coal mining industry on its feet, so that it would not need to go cap in hand to the government asking other areas and industries to contribute to its support. Had the minister in his speech given us any suggestions along these lines there would have been some comfort for us in British Columbia. I specifically asked what hope he could hold out. However, anyone who reads Hansard will readily see that he had no solutions whatever to offer.

For a moment I should like to turn to another feature of coal mining in British Columbia, concerning a condition which obtains in a constituency I do not represent. On April 5, more than a month ago, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre asked if the attention of the Minister of Mines had been called to the serious condition of the coal industry at Fernie. The whole industry, in fact the whole town, was in the process of being wiped out, owing to the closing of the local mines. The minister replied that the question of what could be done, if anything, had been taken up with the government of British Columbia, upon whom responsibility rested, if there were any responsibility. He went on to say that if it were possible for the government to assist, of course that assistance would be given. The suggestion that the responsibility rested upon the province of British Columbia would apply only to taking care of relief. The minister overlooked, however, or did not seem to realize, the greater responsibility resting upon the dominion of adopting a policy to take care of the situation, especially, as I shall proceed to show, it was the policy of this government which brought Fernie to the desperate point it has now reached. I say that at least in part-and I think a large part-the government policy brought about that situation. Hon. members from the east will understand better if I explain that Fernie is in that part of British Columbia bordering on the United States and practically ninety per cent of its coal output went to that country. The government's policy adopted last year of raising the duty on coal coming into Canada, which automatically raised the duty on coal going into the United States, resulted in the total loss of that foreign trade, which amounted to about ninety per cent of the total. I quote from a well known Conservative paper in British Columbia:
The manipulation of reciprocal tariffs on coal, while beneficial to eastern Canadian coal operators, Fernie mines suffered severely as 90 per cent of its markets which were export, were completely shut off.
Another says:
One of the contributing causes for the railroads doing this-
That is ceasing to take the coal.
-may be assigned to the imposition of increased duty on coal going into the United States, which was put into force as a countervailing duty on Canadian exports. The application of this duty reduced the number of employees at Coal Creek to the extent of 300.
The town, which numbers some 4,000 inhabitants, is practically bankrupt. People will
JMr. Natl.]
have to move away or be kept on relief, because it is just a one industry town.
Now we were told-until I was sick of hearing of it-on every platform in my riding during the last election, that it was not right to take the narrow view I was taking of looking after the interests of Comox-Alberni first. The electors were invited to take a broad national view; a broad national policy was the idea. I predicted at that time, with almost alarming accuracy as it has proved, that that would merely mean the sacrifice of the British Columbia miners for the benefit of Alberta or of eastern coal areas. That is exactly what has taken place. "Wide is the road and broad the way that leadeth to destruction, and many there be that walk therein"-principally I think because it is the easiest; they follow the line of least resistance. That is what happened in this case.
Did you say the other road is straight?

I did not deal with the other road; I leave that to the member for Wey-burn-I wish he were on it now. I do not say the result was the government's fault; they certainly did not do it deliberately, but as part of a national policy which may have secured great advantages for Nova Scotia and Alberta. I do not even say that the policy was wrong, but when they saw the situation that was likely to arise they should have acted on item 8, I think it was, of the policy of the Conservative party in the last election, and provided compensating adjustments. That could easily have been done by increasing the bonus on the Crowsnest coal so that it could have got into some of the central Canadian markets.
That then, is the situation. What are we doing about it? As far as I can make out, nothing. As far as I can make out, we are going to do nothing. The days are passing into weeks, the weeks into months and the months into years, yet we are dallying along the primrose path, taking the line of least resistance. We stop here and there and gather a flower of trite truisms or pick a posy of platitudes; we go on down the path of dolce far niente into the great Never-Never land where it is always afternoon, where the shadows are always long, where people live in a vague, misty haze, a narrow confined area surrounded by nebulous and unsubstantial hopes, where "man never is but always to be blessed." When I refer to the minister in this connection I do not know that that is fair, I should perhaps say his department; and even then I should limit it-I mean the

Supply-M ines-Coal
ooal mines branch of the Department of Mines. They seem always to have the backward look; they are the apostles of precedent, ever looking timorously behind them for some precedent to guide them. But these are days of change; why do they not get out and make precedents? Instead of being, and leaving us to be, the victims of circumstances, why do they not seize the circumstances and compel them to serve their end and ours, compel them to produce a policy that will meet the situation? Why do they not make things happen? The Prime Minister on an occasion in his earlier career immortalized himself, pounded the desk, I am told, and said that either he or the government would make things happen. That is what we want done. To use a vernacular expression, the minister needs to shake up his department and tell them to get a move on. I suggest that his department requires a new motto, a new slogan. The motto should be "requiescat in pace," and the slogan: "yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep." Yes, and it needs only some sympathetic friend to put a lily in its hand; then the coal mining industry of Vancouver island would be in a position to say: Don't it look nat'ral? -and I might add, appropriate.
In my opening words this afternoon I did not go any further than ask the minister if he could give us any suggestion, any encouragement, any hope of any policy or any action in this regard. Had he done so I should have been satisfied and said no more. But anyone who will read the minister's reply will be compelled to admit that surely it is time someone butted in, that someone stirred up the stagnant waters, that-someone endeavoured to galvanize the Dead sea fruit of inefficiency and inactivity into energized action. I am not one of those who say I think the government ought to do something, but is unable to suggest what that something should be. I have suggested it.
What more can I say? I see the Prime Minister is in his seat; I will appeal to him. I wonder if he can hold out some hope of reciprocity with the United States that would help us. I know that any view to which he would give expression would not be an accomplished fact, it would be nothing more than a hope, but even hope, however slight and distant, would be better than the black despair which now hangs over the coal mining industry of Vancouver island and British Columbia generally. I am not speaking for the sake of attacking the minister; I have nothing to gain by that. I am only making an earnest endeavour to galvanize if possible
the government into action, to impress upon the government-I wish I had greater power to express it-the desperateness of the situation, in case happily I might bring the government to a realization of the extreme importance of taking early and speedy action in this matter.

Can the minister tell us whether in addition to this $2,000,000 that is being provided by the tax payer for the moving of this coal, the railways contribute anything in the form of lower freight rates?
No, there has been no contribution as far as lower freight rates are concerned with respect to coal.

The regular rate is applied. Can the minister tell us further if all of this money has been spent on freight rates or if some of it has been spent in other ways? How much has gone for administration? Has anything gone for research or any other kind of work?
Out of an expenditure of $1,750,000 an amount of $15,000 has gone for administration.
And all the rest has gone to the railway companies?
No, to the producers of the coal, but applied towards the reduction of the rate, of course.

I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the suggestions he made for improving the situation of the coal mining industry in western Canada. He made four suggestions: first that the government lend assistance to devising some way of processing the coal so that it will be more acceptable to the market. Something might be said in favour of that, but our experience with processing coal has not been very fortunate in the past. Some years ago the federal government in conjunction with the Manitoba^ government and1 the Saskatchewan government established a plant in southern Saskatchewan to experiment in the processing of lignite coal with a view to making it more marketable. I think millions were spent in that enterprise. Finally when they thought they had something accomplished they handed the whole plant over to a syndicate of capitalists-gave it to them for a dollar, I believe, the government withdrawing from the field. This syndicate, not satisfied with getting the plant for nothing, then asked the government to buy their output. I know the Saskat-
Supply-M in es-Coal

chewan government undertook to supply their public building with the product at a price profitable to the owners. But still they were not satisfied; I never yet knew any industry built on subventions and grants to be satisfied, and I doubt if anyone else in this country ever heard of such a thing. Feed them on pap, subventions, favours of one kind and another, and they always come asking for more.
The member for Comox-Alberni also suggested increasing the subventions. I say again, when can you satisfy an industry by increasing subventions? The more you give them the more they want. They seem to have only one word in their vocabulary; that is the word "more". No matter what you give them they always cry for more, and these industries are always in distress. Look at what has been done for the steel and coal industry in Nova Scotia, but has there ever been a session of this parliament when they have not been crying for more? Certainly there has not been such a session since I came here. Then the hon. member for Comox-Alberni also suggested that we might stop the importation of cheap coal from Great Britain.
To the Pacific.

Why should we prohibit the importation of cheap coal from any country? When Great Britain became the leading industrial country in the world it was largely because she had the cheapest coal. Wheu Germany became a great industrial nation one of the main reasons was that she had great coal deposits within her own borders. When the eastern central United States developed the same industrial enterprises it was also largely because they had cheap coal. Why should we deny our people this essential to the building up of industry? I think it would be folly in the extreme. If Great Britain sees fit to bonus her coal exports, so much the better for us; if she wants to tax her people in order to give us the cheap fuel we need, so much the better for us.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni made one suggestion, however, and because of that I am willing to forgive him all the rest; he suggested reciprocity with the United States with regard to coal. Think what it would mean to this country if we had reciprocity with the United States, even if it were only with regard to coal. Look at the great industrial portion of Canada just across the lakes from some of the richest coal deposits in the world. Coal can be brought in from the United States at a cost of a little over SI. 50 per ton. Then look at the western coast where the coal deposits are on our side of the f.Mr. Young.]
line and the natural market is on the other side. It is reported that the Prime Minister is going to arrange some sort of reciprocity treaty with the United States. One of the very best provisions he could include in that treaty would be reciprocity in coal.
And fish.

Yes, and fish if you like.
That would give central Canada the cheap coal from the United States, and it would afford the people of western Canada a market for their coal.

In that case what
would happen the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia?
In what condition is the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia at present?
It would be wiped off the map.

The coal mines in Nova
Scotia are on the seaboard. If we had reciprocity would there be anything to stop the exportation of coal to the United States?
Certainly; they cannot land it in the United States to compete with their domestic coal.
Is it not true also that United States coal is more suitable for the purposes for which it is required?
No.
Is it not true that the people of Nova Scotia burn United States coal in their stoves?
No.

Yes, it is true; they prefer it. If the people of Nova Scotia persist in bringing coal from under the sea when they can get it cheaper somewhere else I do not know that it is the duty of this government to encourage them in that uneconomic practice. This afternoon the minister spoke of the high price he had to pay for United States coal at one time, and he said he did not want to bring about that condition again.
I also paid those high prices, but I know- and I think the minister knows-that it was war time, and we were paying war prices. I can also tell the minister that while commodity prices have been going down the price of coal has not gone down to nearly the same degree.

If I might interrupt my hon. friend to say so, the main reason is that throughout the world the wage scales of coal

Supply-Mines-Coal
miners have not been reduced, and I do not think the hon. member would suggest that they should be reduced.
Then the minister says that the coal miners are getting better wages, that they are the only basic producers whose wages have not been reduced?
They have been reduced, but not to the same extent.
Why should they be reduced when we are voting 82,000,000 out of the treasury to assist that industry?

Perhaps their wages have not been reduced but their working hours certainly have been cut down. In one case men have been working only three days in a fortnight, and I should say that was quite a reduction.

Yes, but perhaps if they were working at a lower rate they would get more work. The hon. member for Comox-Alberai spoke of hungry miners; that is what he is thinking of. I am thinking of shivering consumers, people who cannot buy coal in a country where they need it, people who cannot buy fuel and who do not know where to get the money with which to keep themselves warm. Here we are taxing ourselves to the extent of $2,000,000 extra in order to keep coal out of this country. The minister says he is afraid of a monopoly. What is he doing? He is closing one source of supply in the United States; he has closed another source in Russia and now it is suggested that he should Close still another source in Great Britain and deliver us into the hands of the Canadian coal producers. This afternoon the minister made reference to an eastern and a western coal combine, but now his proposal is to deliver us into the hands of these combines. If he is afraid of a monopoly why deliver us into their hands?
Then there is another point to be considered. If we were getting in coal from the United States the boats carrying grain down the lakes could bring coal back; they would have a cargo both ways, and the result would be lower freight rates on wheat. But when you prohibit the importation of coal from the United States the boats have to come back light, so they must make enough going down to pay for both trips. The result is higher rates on wheat and higher prices for coal. Because of this legislation the farmers of the western provinces, and particularly the farmers of Saskatchewan, will have to sit at their doors and see trainloads of coal passing by going to the eastern provinces, on which they are paying the freight rates though they
get no assistance in connection with their own coal, for which they have to pay the full rate.
The remarks of the minister this afternoon bring up the question as to how far it is the duty of a government to guarantee that industry shall never change. When new methods come into being or new commodities come on the market to compete with those we have been in the habit of using, is it the function or the duty of the government so to arrange things that these new commodities shall not have a chance, by forcing the people to continue to use the old? Let us consider for a moment what would have happened a country whose government always assumed the attitude that they must never allow any change or any progressive thing to happen. What would have happened to a country if, we will say, when printing was first invented they had promptly proceeded to bonus the old fashioned writers in order that the old methods might not be done away with? Supposing when the spinning jenny and loom were invented the same country had promptly proceeded to bonus the old fashioned method of making cloth by hand; what would have happened? What would have been the result if, when matches were invented, they had put a subvention or bounty on the manufacture and use of flint and steel? When steamboats were invented what would have happened if they had started to pay subventions or bounties on boats propelled by oars, or if when railroads were invented, in order to encourage the old industry they had granted subventions on ox carts in order to keep us travelling in that way? When electric lights were invented what would have happened if governments had said, "We will stick to the old tallow candles and force the people to use them"? Where would we be to-day if, when the binder was invented, the government had decided to pay bounties on the old scythes or if, when the thresher was invented, they had decided not to use this modern invention which might throw somebody out of work and had put a bounty on the old fashioned flail? What would have happened if a nation had consistently followed that policy? You may say it could not have happened, because no nation could have survived under those conditions, and that is quite true. Any nation that attempted to do so would have passed on its way long ago, like the mammoth and the dinosaur, and would have been replaced by something more modern.
So I ask the question, Mr. Chairman: Is it the function of the government to preserve the obsolete in industry and say to the people
Supply-Mines-Coal

that no matter what new thing may come along they will see that the existing industry is not harmed? Would it not be much better to say, "If you cannot compete with this new process your industry is out of date and you had better get out of it"? That is the only true law of progress and it is not the function of government to stand in the way of progress and perpetuate the obsolete. It seems to me that the only way to help any industry is to allow it to make progress and expose it to whatever competition the world provides.
Would that be correct with regard to the wheat industry of western Canada?
Yes.
Then you should have received better prices than you did receive in the past year.
Are you going to raise prices by your tariffs?

We have raised
them already.

You put on a duty of
thirty cents and the price went lower than ever. For several years past every government in the world has been bending every effort to try to bolster up the price of wheat. The net result of all these efforts has been lower prices than ever. This afternoon I made a motion which I understand was out of order; I -moved that this item be struck out entirely. I am now going to make one which is in order; I move tha-t it be reduced to one dollar.

I shall not take up the
time of the committee at any great length in connection with this item but I would like to make a few observations on what the hon. member for Weybum has said with respect to this industry. In the first place, the hon. member advocates the removal of duties on coal and claims that this action would result in Nova Scotia coal being burned in the eastern United States. I suggest that the hon. member look at the prices prevailing in the consuming markets along the Atlantic seaboard in the United States. He will find that it would be impossible for those states to provide a market for Nova Scotia coal. The hon. member then argued that by taking off the tariff the coal from British Columbia could go down to Washington, Utah and other western states and provide a solution for the whole problem.

No, I did not say that.
TMr. Young.]

An examination of the
cost of producing coal at Bellingham will show that the general costs are much lower than those of British Columbia, including Vancouver island.
The Seattle coal is very inferior.

The Bellingham coal may be inferior but the Utah coal certainly is not. I have reviewed this matter and I feel sure that that market would not be available to us.
I do not know* that I would care to quarrel very much with -the theory advanced by the hon. member of making every industry and every vocation, public or private, stand upon its own feet and get along without assistance. When -time has permitted, I have listened to the debates in this house and I have come to the conclusion -that it all depends upon where a man lives or where his interest may be when it comes to deciding to what extent he will Stamp with his approval an invasion of the public treasury. I did not hear the hon. member for Weybum stand up-he may have done it-and deplore the paving of a bonus on wheat.
He did, though.

If he did, then I compliment him upon his consistency. During the debates which have taken place in this house upon tariffs, bonuses and things of that character, there has been disclosed an attitude of silence by hon. members when such matters touch their particular geographical locality or something in which they are interested.
I might tell my hon. friend that we have coal deposits in my constituency.

Yes. I understand the Truax Traer property is located in my hon. friend's constituency. We find the hon. member for Comox-Albemi impeaching the government for everything it has done with respect to the assistance given to the coal industry on Vancouver island.
For what they have not done.

I do not expect anything else because that has always been his attitude ever since I have had anything to do with the administration of the Mines department. From year to year I have had occasion to examine in-to the difficulties facing this industry and, as I have said before, I realize that there is a limit to which the government can go in giving assistance to the coal or any other industry. As I said a moment ago, I am not quarrelling with those who condemn the

Supply-Mines-C oal
bemusing of industries and things of that character, but we must realize that there are industries which are vital to the life of this country, particularly during times like these. If these industries cannot prevail without something more than sympathetic interest on the part of the government, if they are left to get along on their own at a time like this, then I would fear greatly for the tens of thousands of workmen who are dependent upon them for their livelihood. The hon. member for Coimox-Alberni has always adopted a consistent attitude with regard to these matters. Perhaps that is his duty, occupying the position he does in this house. I have discussed this question with those most vitally interested, with those who have huge investments on the island and although it may not be the fault of those at present in control of the industry, the fact is that the past history reveals that the expenditures and expansions which have taken place were not to be commended. I have had many conferences with those in control of this industry. Is it possible that they are not interested in their mines? Of course they are. Is it possible that they are not doing their best to make their mines pay? Of course they are. But it is equally true that in common with the rest of the world, Canada's consumption of coal has been going down for almost four years. However, as I said this afternoon, the figures disclose that Canada has not suffered as much as other countries. I had a conference with the operators of Vancouver island over three years ago. They asked for certain assistance which would enable them to maintain their men in employment. That assistance, which may be in definance of the theory advocated by the hon. member for Weyburn, was granted by the government. Unfortunately they did not properly forecast the future, and the consumption of coal fell off. As everyone knows, they again approached the government asking for further assistance and this was granted with respect to 'bunker and export coal. The export market is mainly in South America because in order to ship in the United States they would have to meet the Same duty which we impose. It was the considered view at the time of those in charge of those operations on Vancouver island that the assistance given by the government to those mine owners would enable them to keep their workmen employed and to maintain that industry on its feet. Again consumption fell off and to-day they are having an extremely difficult time.
When I made reference a few weeks ago, when this item was before the committee, to
the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I did not do so or intend to do so in a way that would cause him to feel aggrieved; if I did,
I am indeed sorry for it. But when this matter was engaging the attention of the Canadian Collieries Limited and myself, I received unsolicited a letter from the general manager. I shall not place it on Hansard, but it was a letter to which I made reference before. In the view of those who are in charge of the coal mining industry on Vancouver island, the efforts of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni were not helpful and they so state in their communication to me. They may be wrong and his efforts may have been very helpful, but that was their opinion. I have it from the producers of coal on Vancouver island that as a result of the assistance which the government has given them, they have been able to keep their miners working at least on part time. It is true that they are having great and serious difficulties.
So far as the importation of British coal is concerned, that has amounted to only some 9,600 tons. That in itself is not of any great importance.
In two months.

Yes. I do not care to
dwell on that any further.
Since I have come into the house the hon, member for Comox-Albemi has not dealt with me in any particularly friendly way in connection with any of these coal matters. On almost every occasion, with his facility of expression and his subtlety in debate, he has turned his attack on me and he has never failed, when matters in connection with the coal industry have come up, to go the whole length in condemning anything the government sought to do.
